episode_title: Ep. 120 Mohamed Samir: From P&G to Halwani Brothers CEO: A Leadership Journey Across Four Decades

real_qa.q: What was Mohamed Samir's career path from Procter & Gamble to becoming CEO of Halwani Brothers?
real_qa.r: Mohamed Samir spent 30 years with Procter & Gamble starting in 1989, then had a couple of stints with regional companies, did consultancy work for a couple of years before discovering it was not his cup of tea, and for the past eight months has been CEO of Halwani Brothers, a food company based in Saudi Arabia.
real_qa.requete: Mohamed Samir CEO Halwani Brothers career

real_qa.q: How did growing up in multiple countries shape Mohamed Samir's approach to cross-cultural leadership?
real_qa.r: Mohamed Samir learned that although there are many similarities between people from different parts of the world, small differences matter greatly. He discovered that the way you say things and how people react varies significantly by country—for example, in the UK saying 'not too bad' means 'amazing,' while in the US 'awesome' might just mean 'okay.' Learning how to cope with these cultural nuances became a very important part of his leadership approach.

real_qa.q: What was Mohamed Samir's personal vision written in 1991 and how did it shape his career decisions?
real_qa.r: In 1991, Mohamed Samir wrote down a handwritten holistic vision with three main components: making his children better than him, helping others succeed especially when they are out of a job, and achieving specific professional targets with timelines plus financial independence to stick to his principles. He has kept this handwritten vision and continued referring back to it throughout his 30+ year career, still working to deliver all of it.

real_qa.q: What was the Corporate Athlete training lesson about vision that stuck with Mohamed Samir?
real_qa.r: During a Corporate Athlete training where the average group age was 42 years old, the trainer pointed out that the group had 42 years to write down their vision but wanted five more minutes, illustrating that people need to spend real time on things that make a difference in their direction. Mohamed Samir learned that if you don't know where you're going, you'll never know whether you achieved it through effort or luck.

real_qa.q: How did the loss of his father at age 23 influence Mohamed Samir's approach to family time and work-life balance?
real_qa.r: When Mohamed Samir's father passed away when he was 23, it shaped his belief that quality time with family matters more than quantity. He developed the principle of 'people before machines and one machine at a time'—putting his phone down when his kids want to talk, not talking on the phone while driving. He learned early that the worst thing to hear from children is 'we wish you spent more time with us,' and as long as they don't say that, he considers it acceptable.
real_qa.requete: work-life balance family time quality attention

real_qa.q: What two core principles did Mohamed Samir focus on for running a business in his 40s?
real_qa.r: In his 40s, Mohamed Samir decided to focus on only two things for running a business: make decisions for the long term while delivering the quarter and month, and take care of the people so they take care of the business. He learned from his mentor that he needed to let go and allow his people to do more of the things he was used to doing, even if they made mistakes, because this was the only way to grow.
real_qa.requete: long-term decision making people management leadership

guest.bio_context: Mohamed Samir spent 30 years working with Procter & Gamble starting in 1989, developing extensive expertise in FMCG marketing and leadership across multiple countries. He held several country manager and regional positions before transitioning through regional companies and consultancy roles. He has been CEO of Halwani Brothers, a food company based in Saudi Arabia, for the past eight months at the time of this interview.

real_quote: If you're not happy going to work every morning, then it's time to move on somewhere else. But don't stay and feel that you don't want to spend more time there.
